claims.title: Shopper order data may be intercepted if public order transport is not encrypted
claims.description: `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order` crosses from `boundary:public-internet` to `boundary:storefront-dmz` and carries order contents, shipping addresses, and card last-four values. Its `encryption_in_transit` is unknown. If this transport is not protected, an attacker able to observe the shopper-to-API path can intercept those order records before they reach `process:storefront-api`. The disclosed shopper and order identifiers can enable targeted fraud or correlation with records subsequently handled by `process:order-service` and `store:orders-db`; this is conditional on resolving the unknown transport control as absent or ineffective.

quotes.text: Shoppers sign in with email and password and get a session cookie; we have not rolled out MFA for shopper accounts yet.
Orders, shopper addresses and card-last-four live in a PostgreSQL database (orders-db)

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional because `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order` crosses the public-internet boundary but its `encryption_in_transit` is unknown, so an attacker still needs an on-path position. Impact is high because the flow carries `pii` and `financial` order data, including shipping addresses and card last-four values.

mitigations.summary: Require TLS for shopper order submission
mitigations.detail: Verify and enforce TLS 1.2+ on `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order`, redirect plaintext attempts, and record the verified transport posture in `encryption_in_transit`.

mitigations.summary: Minimize payment data on the order flow
mitigations.detail: Replace card-related values with processor-issued opaque references where the storefront does not need to handle the underlying value.

claims.title: Settlement details may be intercepted if the processor webhook transport is unprotected
claims.description: `flow:entity:card-processor>process:storefront-api>settlement-webhook` crosses from `boundary:public-internet` to `boundary:storefront-dmz`, carries financial settlement-confirmation data, and has unknown protocol and `encryption_in_transit`. If the callback is sent without effective transport encryption, an on-path attacker can intercept payment-settlement information before it reaches `process:storefront-api`. This can reveal which orders have been paid and provide information for targeted social engineering or order fraud; the draft is conditional because the transport was not stated.

quotes.text: After they settle a payment they POST a webhook back to the storefront API to tell us the order is paid.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional because the webhook crosses the public-internet boundary while both its protocol and `encryption_in_transit` are unknown, but interception still requires an on-path position. Impact is medium because the flow is tagged `financial` and exposes payment-settlement status, rather than the full order corpus.

mitigations.summary: Require authenticated TLS for processor callbacks
mitigations.detail: Require HTTPS with modern TLS for `flow:entity:card-processor>process:storefront-api>settlement-webhook`, reject plaintext callback delivery, and document the verified transport setting.

mitigations.summary: Limit settlement data to opaque order references
mitigations.detail: Ensure the callback carries only the minimum processor status and an opaque order reference, with no shopper or payment details in URLs or headers.

claims.title: Order contents may be intercepted on the unverified DMZ-to-core gRPC channel
claims.description: `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order` crosses from `boundary:storefront-dmz` to `boundary:core-services` and carries order contents, shopper identifiers, and shipping addresses. The flow has `encryption_in_transit: unknown`. If the gRPC channel lacks effective TLS, an attacker able to observe this inter-zone path can intercept the PII and financial order data sent from `process:storefront-api` to `process:order-service`. The identifiers can be correlated with rows later read and written through `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders`; this is conditional on the unverified encryption state.

quotes.text: When a shopper submits an order the storefront API calls the order service over gRPC.
Orders, shopper addresses and card-last-four live in a PostgreSQL database (orders-db)

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional because the flow is a stated DMZ-to-core boundary crossing and its `encryption_in_transit` is unknown, although the attacker must obtain an on-path position. Impact is high because the flow carries `pii` and `financial` data for submitted orders, including shopper identifiers and addresses.

mitigations.summary: Use mTLS on the gRPC order-submission channel
mitigations.detail: Set `encryption_in_transit` for `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order` to mTLS so both the order payload and service peer identity are protected.
Segment the DMZ-to-core path and limit diagnostics, sidecars, and infrastructure identities that can capture traffic on this channel.

claims.title: Order database traffic may expose shopper records if its transport protection is absent
claims.description: `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders` carries order rows, shipping addresses, and card last-four values to `store:orders-db`, but its protocol and `encryption_in_transit` are unknown. If the database connection is not protected, an attacker with a position on the core-services network path can intercept records exchanged between `process:order-service` and `store:orders-db`. The captured identifiers and payment-related fields enable targeted attacks against shoppers and correlation with the confidential database corpus; this is conditional and does not assert that the database connection is plaintext.

quotes.text: Orders, shopper addresses and card-last-four live in a PostgreSQL database (orders-db) that the order service reads and writes

severity.justification: Likelihood is low and conditional because the connection is inside `boundary:core-services`, so an attacker needs a prior on-path foothold as well as the unknown transport protection resolving unfavorably. Impact is high because the flow handles the confidential `store:orders-db` corpus tagged `pii` and `financial`.

mitigations.summary: Enforce TLS for the database connection
mitigations.detail: Configure PostgreSQL TLS with certificate validation for `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders` and reject non-TLS connections.

mitigations.summary: Use separate database credentials with mutual identity verification
mitigations.detail: Bind the order service's database identity to the authenticated TLS connection so intercepted connection material cannot be reused elsewhere.

claims.title: A copied orders database may disclose confidential records if encryption at rest is absent
claims.description: `store:orders-db` is classified confidential, contains `pii` and `financial` assets, and has `encryption_at_rest: unknown`. If that unknown resolves to storage without effective encryption, an attacker who obtains a database volume, snapshot, backup, or other operational copy can read order rows, shopper addresses, and card last-four values without using `process:order-service` or its normal database connection. This creates corpus-scale disclosure and supplies identifiers that can be used to target shoppers; it is conditional on the unverified at-rest protection and does not claim that the store is currently unencrypted.

quotes.text: Orders, shopper addresses and card-last-four live in a PostgreSQL database (orders-db)

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional because `store:orders-db` has unknown `encryption_at_rest`, and obtaining an operational copy avoids the live application path if encryption is absent. Impact is high because the store is confidential and tagged `pii` and `financial`, so one copied artifact can disclose the order corpus.

mitigations.summary: Verify and enforce encryption at rest for orders data
mitigations.detail: Establish the actual `encryption_at_rest` state for `store:orders-db`, then require managed-key encryption for the database and every backup, snapshot, export, and replica.

mitigations.summary: Restrict access to database copies and keys
mitigations.detail: Limit snapshot, backup, restore, and key-use permissions to dedicated principals and monitor bulk export or restore activity.

claims.title: Compromise of the order service exposes the orders database through its broad application grant
claims.description: `process:order-service` reads and writes `store:orders-db` through `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders` using one application account with full read/write authority. An attacker who runs code in `process:order-service` can use that already-authorized database session to read the confidential order corpus, including shopper addresses and card last-four values. Encryption at rest would not stop this attacker because the database serves decrypted records to an authorized application session. The attacker can then use the recovered shopper and order information for targeted fraud; this draft concerns code execution in the reader, not a storage copy or a separately held credential.

quotes.text: the order service reads and writes with a single application account that has full read/write.

severity.justification: Likelihood is low because the attacker must first execute code in internal `process:order-service`; no execution path is stated. Impact is high because its single application account has full read/write access to confidential `store:orders-db`, which contains `pii` and `financial` data.

mitigations.summary: Reduce the order service database grant
mitigations.detail: Replace the full read/write application account with narrowly scoped roles, views, and column permissions that expose only the rows and fields required for order capture.
Log database reads by the order-service identity and alert on bulk extraction, unusual tables, or query volumes inconsistent with normal order processing.

claims.title: A recovered order-service database password enables direct bulk reading of orders
claims.description: The database credential used on `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders` is a single application-account password kept in an environment variable on `process:order-service`, and that account has full read/write access to `store:orders-db`. An attacker who recovers this credential from the worker environment can present it to the database interface and read order rows, shopper addresses, and card last-four values without running code in the order service. The resulting corpus disclosure can be used for targeted fraud and is distinct from the initial credential-recovery action: this draft is the direct database read enabled by holding the password.

quotes.text: The password comes from an environment variable on the worker.
the order service reads and writes with a single application account that has full read/write.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium because the attacker must first obtain the environment-held application password, but it is a standing shared credential rather than a short-lived scoped identity. Impact is high because the password's account has full read/write access to confidential `store:orders-db` containing `pii` and `financial` data.

mitigations.detail: Use workload identity or short-lived database credentials issued to `process:order-service` instead of an environment-variable password.

mitigations.summary: Constrain where the database identity may connect
mitigations.detail: Require the workload identity and approved network path for database sessions, so a recovered password alone cannot be used from an attacker-controlled client.

claims.title: The worker environment can disclose a standing database credential
claims.description: `process:order-service` keeps the application-account password for `store:orders-db` in an environment variable. An attacker who obtains access to the worker runtime, a diagnostic environment dump, or another artifact exposing that environment can recover the credential. Because the account has full read/write authority on the database, the recovered value enables the holder to query `store:orders-db` directly and disclose the shopper and order corpus. This is the credential-disclosure step; use of the recovered password against the database is separately represented by the direct-read threat.

quotes.text: The password comes from an environment variable on the worker.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium because recovery requires access to an environment-bearing worker artifact, but the credential is a long-lived password stored in `process:order-service` rather than a short-lived identity. Impact is high because the recovered credential is accepted by an account with full read/write access to confidential `store:orders-db`.

mitigations.summary: Move the database secret out of the worker environment
mitigations.detail: Use workload federation or a dedicated secret manager with short-lived issuance so the order worker does not retain a reusable database password in its environment.

mitigations.summary: Rotate and scan for exposed credentials
mitigations.detail: Rotate the current application password, prevent it from appearing in diagnostics and logs, and scan build artifacts, images, and runtime-support exports for historical copies.
